objections: Not one of the nine evidence items contains a consensus estimate, an Apple figure, or a forecast. The three 'consensus' queries return only authorship metadata for Cohen/Dey/Lys accounting papers (abstract_inverted_index is null), and the beat/miss-history queries return Zittrain's book abstract matched on the incidental words 'internet', 'stop', 'over'. There is zero evidence of any kind supporting 'above consensus' — no EPS number, no revenue number, no analyst count, not even Apple's fiscal calendar. A conclusion of YES rests on literally nothing; the only defensible output is UNRESOLVED, and any affirmative lean is fabricated from empty retrievals.

The observed pattern — every sub-question returning irrelevant academic works — is fully explained by a broken full-text search pipeline concatenating whole natural-language questions into OpenAlex fulltext.search filters, which retrieves documents sharing generic words ('report', 'quarter', 'apple') rather than financial data. Under this mechanism the 'SPECULATIVE 0.54' label is itself an artifact of the same failure, not a signal about Apple's earnings probability.

OpenAlex indexes academic literature, which by construction contains no live sell-side consensus estimates; querying it for analyst forecasts guarantees null results regardless of what the truth about Apple's quarter is. Any confidence number attached to this conclusion is produced entirely inside a source corpus that structurally cannot contain the deciding fact — survivorship of whatever the retrieval happened to surface, not evidence about earnings.

The single most likely artifact: the 0.54 'SPECULATIVE' score on the first sub-question is being read as mild positive signal toward a beat, when its own text explicitly states the question cannot be answered and a live estimates API would be required. Similarly the OECD green-growth paper's abstract mentions 'performance', 'targets', 'improved' — keyword collisions that a scoring layer could mistake for outlook-relevant content. The conclusion is most plausibly a keyword-coincidence artifact layered on failed retrieval.

objections: There is no conclusion to defend: every constituent answer is UNVERIFIED or SPECULATIVE with zero supporting data (evidence consists solely of OpenAlex records for three unrelated academic papers and four zero-result searches). The headline 'Will Nvidia report above consensus?' was never answered yes or no by any evidence item — the pipeline returned 0.00-0.54 confidence 'cannot be determined' responses, not an affirmative prediction.

The pattern of 'no usable evidence' across all five sub-questions is fully explained by a tool-selection failure: the researcher queried OpenAlex (an academic literature database) for real-time market data that only exists in financial data providers (consensus estimate aggregators, earnings calendars). The absence of Nvidia consensus figures in peer-reviewed literature is expected regardless of the true answer, so the empty evidence base tells us nothing about whether Nvidia will beat.

Full-text search over arXiv/OpenAlex systematically excludes exactly the sources containing the needed facts (analyst estimate databases, press coverage of guidance revisions, hyperscaler earnings calls). The searches were also keyword-stuffed natural-language strings against a fulltext.search filter, which returns near-zero hits by construction — e.g. query 3 and queries 7-8 returned count:0. This guarantees apparent evidential silence independent of reality.

If this record is being read as a calibrated 'unknown' outcome, it is an artifact of retrieval failure, not genuine uncertainty: the same five questions answered via any live market-data source would yield concrete consensus figures and recent beat/miss magnitudes (publicly documented), collapsing the 0.50-0.54 speculative scores into either a grounded prediction or a grounded rejection within minutes. The 'speculative' confidence values themselves are unanchored — nothing in the evidence supports even those numbers.

objections: The evidence base contains zero Boeing data of any kind: no consensus revenue/EPS figures, no earnings date, no delivery counts, no cash flow, no program status. Every retrieval (OpenAlex full-text searches) returned irrelevant academic papers — a Nike Corporate Responsibility Report, a hospital-handoffs literature review, and accounting studies (Li & Lin; Jia, Redigolo, Shu & Zhao; Qiu et al.). There is no fact in the record that could support 'above consensus' even weakly; a single live data point (e.g., a Zacks/Refinitiv consensus showing Boeing's consensus EPS is deeply negative and routinely missed) would refute the conclusion outright, and none was sought from a market-data source.

The most likely artifact is pipeline failure masquerading as a conclusion: the research tool was pointed at OpenAlex (an academic-paper index) instead of a market-data API, so it returned keyword-matched papers whose abstracts merely contain words like 'analysts', 'earnings', and 'consensus'. Any 'above consensus' answer produced from this run is a retrieval-tool artifact, not an inference from evidence — the conclusion should not exist at all, and its existence is itself the false positive.

The searches show classic query-stuffing: the second query appends the authors' names ('yinghua yupeng') to force a match, and several queries returned count=0 or matched only generic boilerplate (the Cohen & Hilligoss handoffs paper matched via repository boilerplate text). This is a multiple-comparisons/keyword-mining pattern: with enough reformulated queries, irrelevant documents matching on shared vocabulary will always surface, creating the appearance of topical support where none exists.

Even absent any Boeing data, the base-rate alternative explains a 'beat' prediction at least as well: sell-side analysts systematically walk down estimates before reports for distressed firms, and companies manage results to clear lowered bars, so 'beat consensus' is the modal outcome for most large caps for reasons having nothing to do with Boeing-specific fundamentals — meaning any observed hit rate of this conclusion would be indistinguishable from the generic analyst-anchoring base rate, not evidence about Boeing.

objections: The evidence base contains zero Tesla-specific financial data of any kind — no revenue figure, no EPS figure, no consensus estimate, no earnings date, not even a Tesla mention outside the query strings themselves. The two final searches (count: 0) returned literally nothing for the exact claim 'Tesla actual reported revenue eps next earnings report exceed prevailing pre release wall street consensus estimates.' A binary prediction ('will exceed consensus') is asserted with no supporting observation whatsoever; any single real data point — e.g., a current Visible Alpha or FactSet consensus number and delivery/production guidance — could refute it, and none was consulted.

The evidence-gathering process searched OpenAlex, an academic-works database, for live market expectations. This is a tool-selection failure that guarantees null evidence regardless of what the market actually prices: analyst consensuses live in Bloomberg/FactSet/S&P Capital IQ/Zacks/Yahoo Finance, not in scholarly full-text search. The pipeline then labeled three unanswerable questions 'SPECULATIVE 0.54' and one 'UNVERIFIED 0.00' — the 0.54 scores are pure artifact of the labeling rubric, not signal; a different retrieval source would have produced entirely different (and answerable) items.

Even if the pipeline intended the academic hits as proxies, they support no directional claim about Tesla. The Li/Lin paper concerns analyst coverage reacting to product-quality failures cross-sectionally; the Koval et al. paper predicts aggregate earnings surprises from transcript language across ~5,000 companies; the Lyle/Yohn paper is about PEAD trading signals on portfolios. None identifies Tesla, none reports historical Tesla surprise frequency, and none yields a point forecast. Any 'yes' verdict would be an inference smuggled in from literature the pipeline itself never connected to the question.

The most likely artifact: a base-rate guess dressed as analysis. Historically Tesla beats EPS consensus most quarters due to conservative analyst anchoring and adjustment-item definitions, so a naive 'yes' can look correct while carrying no evidentiary content from this run. Additionally, 'above consensus' is ambiguous across estimate vendors and GAAP vs non-GAAP EPS — with no consensus source named, even a future outcome check cannot falsify or confirm the call as stated, making the conclusion unfalsifiable rather than supported.
